name: Fever in adults: causes and when to get help
headline: High temperature in adults: what usually causes it and when to get help
summary: A high temperature in adults is usually a sign of infection and often settles at home. The NHS advises urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP if it does not improve, and 999 for some warning signs.
keyPoints: The NHS says a high temperature is usually a symptom of an infection.
Home care in the NHS advice includes resting, drinking fluids and, if needed, taking paracetamol or ibuprofen.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if a high temperature is not improving after home treatment or is getting worse.
The NHS meningitis page says to call 999 or go to A&E for a very painful headache, confusion, a stiff neck with sensitivity to bright lights, or a rash that does not fade when pressed.

body.heading: What causes a high temperature?
body.body: The NHS says a high temperature is usually a symptom of an infection. Infections such as flu and glandular fever can cause a high temperature.

body.heading: What helps at home?
body.body: NHS advice for a high temperature is to rest and drink plenty of fluids. The NHS also says paracetamol or ibuprofen can be taken to help feel more comfortable, following the instructions on the packet or leaflet. NHS inform also suggests wearing loose, comfortable clothing and avoiding alcohol. Staying away from other people while you have a temperature is also advised, to avoid passing on an infection.

body.heading: When is it worth speaking to a GP or NHS 111?
body.body: The NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 if a high temperature is not improving after treating it at home, or is getting worse. NHS 111 is free and open every day of the year, day and night.

body.heading: Which signs mean 999 or A&E?
body.body: The NHS meningitis page lists a rash that does not fade when pressed, a very painful headache, confusion, and a stiff neck with sensitivity to bright lights among the signs that need immediate action. For a rash, the NHS describes the glass test: pressing a clear glass firmly against the skin to see whether the spots fade. Spots that stay visible through the glass are called a non-blanching rash, and rashes can be harder to see on darker skin, so the palms, soles and tummy are worth checking.
